title: Growing beetroot microgreens
subtitle: Striking deep-red cotyledons with an earthy beetroot flavour, cut in 10 to 14 days
excerpt: Beetroot microgreens have some of the most visually striking cotyledons in the microgreen range: deep red stems and seed leaves that hold their colour when cut. The flavour is earthy and mildly sweet, characteristic of beetroot. Cycle is 10 to 14 days.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Beetroot microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop with a 10 to 14 day cycle. Sow on a pre-dampened seed compost tray, blackout for three to four days, then grow in light until the cotyledons are 5 to 8 cm tall. The stems and seed leaves are deep red on most varieties; yellow and striped varieties produce different colour combinations. The earthy flavour is milder than full-grown beetroot.

Note that beetroot seed is a corky cluster that usually contains two or more seeds. This means germination is clustered: a single sown piece produces multiple seedlings. Germination rates can appear lower than other crops because each visible shoot may represent only part of the seed cluster.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. A grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours per day is recommended in winter. The red pigmentation develops in light; beetroot microgreens kept in low light remain pale and produce weaker flavour.
Temperature: 16 to 22°C. Beetroot microgreens tolerate a moderate temperature range; they perform adequately at 15°C but do best between 18 and 22°C.

Day 0: sow. Fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter beetroot seed clusters at 20 to 25 g per 25 cm tray. Press firmly into contact with the medium. Some growers pre-soak beetroot seed for 4 to 6 hours to speed up germination; it helps but is not essential.

Days 1 to 4: blackout. Cover with a second tray, lightly weighted. Beetroot germinates more slowly than brassicas; the blackout phase runs three to four days. Remove when the majority of shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm.
Day 5 onward: light. The red pigmentation in the stems and cotyledons develops within 24 to 48 hours of moving to a bright position.
daily: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water. Remove excess after 30 minutes.

Days 10 to 14: cut. When cotyledons are fully open, vivid red, and 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium. Rinse gently under cold water; the juice stains surfaces and hands. Refrigerate for up to two days in a sealed container.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on beetroot microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Clustered shoots instead of even coverage
items.cause: Beetroot seed is a multi-germ cluster; each piece germinates as a group.
items.fix: This is normal. Spread seed clusters more widely on the next attempt to give each cluster space. Some growers rub the clusters between their palms to partially separate the individual seeds before sowing.

items.symptom: Green or pale cotyledons instead of red
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or increase grow-light intensity. Some yellow or golden beetroot varieties will always produce yellow or cream cotyledons, not red.

items.cause: The corky seed coat is slow to absorb water in dry conditions.
items.fix: Pre-soak the seed in room-temperature water for 4 to 6 hours before sowing on the next attempt. Ensure the seed compost is thoroughly pre-dampened.

content.text: Use untreated beetroot seed. Check the packet before buying; some commercial beetroot seed carries a seed dressing. Deep red varieties (Detroit Dark Red, Bulls Blood) produce the most visually striking microgreens. Yellow or Chioggia varieties produce differently coloured cotyledons.
risk is low to moderate. Bottom-water only and keep the room ventilated during the longer blackout period.
